newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh broadcasters row with govt over frequencies.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh broadcasters row with govt over frequencies.

text.p: Independent broadcasters in Kazakhstan accused the government on Wednesday of political censorship in a row over who rules the airwaves in the capital Almaty.

The frequencies of four independent radio stations were switched off last week, officially for technical reasons ranging from overcrowded airwaves to interference with the city airport's air traffic control.
"Now it is clear these technical causes were no more than a screen," said Mukhtar Ismailov, director of an association of independent broadcasters in the Central Asian region.
"This is the first step to a state dictatorship in the information sector," he said in a statement issued to journalists.

The government flatly denies any political motive for silencing the four radio stations - Radio M, Radio NS, Radio Rik and Radio Totem -- all of which have broadcast forceful stories on the republic's post-Soviet hardships.

"There is absolutely no political cause," said Ilyas Utenbayev, a senior official at the Kazakh communications ministry. "In Almaty the radio and television frequencies are simply very crowded," he told Reuters.
Two of the four were back on air on Wednesday but Radio M and Radio Totem remained silent.

Private broadcasters blossomed after independence from Moscow in 1991, with Almaty boasting seven independent radio stations and eight private television channels. They compete with two state-owned radio stations and television channels.

Amid the steady flow of pop music and advertisments for Thai holidays and French cosmetics, the stations transmit popular reportage on government corruption and the increasingly tough life in Kazakhstan's energy and cash-starved regions.
Kazakhstan's media also operate in a nation where political opposition to strong-man President Nursultan Nazarbayev, the republic's Soviet-era Communist Party boss, is weak.
Sergei Duvanov, head of Radio M, said: "This is an attack on democracy with only one aim -- to close the mouth of independent broadcasters."
Also at issue is a tender next year of radio frequencies. Existing private stations fear losing their licences.

"The bureaucrats want to kill time and shut down private radio stations before the tender," said Rozlana Taukina, head of Radio Totem. "But all independent radio stations have paid their rent and taxes while state broadcasters have debts," she added.
But Utenbayev rejected the charges, saying the tender would enable the government to raise cash to replace ageing state broadcasting equipment.
"Frequencies are up for sale for commercial needs in all civilised countries," Utenbayev said.
